headline: Cockenoe on the Last Ebb: Fluke to 6 Pounds, Porgies Stacked on the Cows
subhead: Warm water has the reef program running on low-light windows and softening tide — here's where I'm putting my anchor this week.
body_markdown:
I made a call Saturday morning I don't make often — I skipped Penfield entirely and ran straight to Cockenoe. Not because Penfield's dead, but because it was 9 a.m. on a bluebird weekend and the mooring field off Southport was already staging six center consoles and a charter boat for the same piece of rock. Cockenoe's reef edge, on the other hand, drops off clean into 15-18 feet of water on the southwest corner, and it doesn't get the same foot traffic because half the fleet doesn't know the drift line. That's the kind of math I do every weekend now — where's the structure that fires on my tide window and doesn't have three boats parked on top of it.

The fluke bite off that Cockenoe edge has been the most consistent thing in my zone all week. Last two hours of the ebb into the top of the tide change, the current sweeps bait off the reef crown and stacks fluke right on the drop where 8 feet turns into 18. I've been dragging 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow, right on bottom, letting the boat do the work on the drift. Took a 6-pound doormat Tuesday on that exact program, and we had four keepers in about ninety minutes before the tide went slack and the bite just shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's fluke fishing right now — tight windows, not all-day grinding.

Kings Point is reading 72.9 degrees, and that warmth is exactly why the daytime bass bite has gone quiet on top. Stripers are doing what they do in early August — holding deep on the hard structure through the sun hours and only coming up to feed at the edges of the day. Sheffield Island's channel, that 15-to-20-foot cut on the north side, has been the spot for that. I've had two solid sessions there right at last light, live-lining peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig with just enough weight to keep it down in the current, and both nights the fish showed in the last 45 minutes before full dark. Nothing huge — mid-20s to low-30-inchers — but consistent enough that I'd plan around it again this week.

We flagged this pattern last week — said that as the tides softened, bass would compress into the tightest current windows and hold on the deepest, coolest structure. That's exactly what's playing out at Sheffield and off Greenwich Point right now. The bite isn't spread out anymore. It's a 45-minute window on the ebb or right at dusk, and if you're not there for it, you're just trolling around in empty water.

The porgy bite on the Cows has been the bright spot for anyone who wants steady action without needing a perfect tide. That shallow structure off Stamford floods hard on the incoming, and porgies pile onto the mussel beds once there's three or four feet of water covering the rocks. Hi-lo rigs with sandworm or squid strips, small hooks, light enough weight to feel the bottom without snagging — we've been loading the cooler with porgies in the 10-to-13-inch class on the flood, best two hours before and after high water. It's not glamorous fishing but it's the most reliable thing going in the western Sound right now, and it's a great option when the weekend boat traffic makes the reef proper unworkable.

Black sea bass have been holding true to form on the rockier structure — Penfield's deeper flanks, 20-25 feet, and the rubble off Greenwich Point. Squid strips or Gulp saltwater shrimp on a knocker rig, bounced right on bottom. It's a grind-it-out fishery this time of year, nothing spectacular, but if you're patient you'll pick through shorts to find enough keepers for dinner. I'd fish it on a slower stage of the tide, not dead high or dead low, because that's when the fish seem to actually feed instead of just sitting tight to the rocks.

Bluefish have been following the bunker pods, and where those pods concentrate off Greenwich Point and the outer Norwalk Islands, the blues show up fast and don't stick around long. It's bait-driven entirely — no bunker, no blues. When I've found working birds over a pod near the Cows, a top-water popper or a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig has produced quick, violent action for twenty minutes before the school moves. Worth having a rod rigged and ready, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it — plan around structure and let the blues be a bonus.

We're heading into the neap around August 5-6, and that's going to soften current across the board — Cockenoe, Penfield, the cut at Sheffield, all of it. When that happens I'll be dropping jig weights and slowing presentations, because a weak push means bait doesn't get swept off structure as hard, and fish get lazier about chasing it. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the last two hours of the ebb at Cockenoe for fluke, then swing to Sheffield right at dusk for a shot at bass on bunker. Keep an eye on boat traffic on the weekend — the reefs that get pounded by 10 a.m. Saturday are dead water by noon, and the smart move is either getting there at first light or finding the piece of structure nobody else bothered to learn.
